newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa's Eskom mulls power plants in mine shafts.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa's Eskom mulls power plants in mine shafts.

text.p: South African power utility Eskom is studying the possibility of using the country's numerous disused mineshafts to generate peak-hour electricity with falling water, officials said.

Eskom spokesman Peter Adams said the theory was that the water, which occurs naturally at the bottom of mines, would be pumped to the surface during off-peak hours then released back down the shaft to drive a turbine generator and help to meet peak demand.
One of the scientists working on the project, Dave Blake, said research was at an early stage.
"We're doing reconaissance studies at the moment. The technology is fairly site specific. You need to find your site and then see if the whole thing comes together," Blake said.
"We're looking at where we could find a site to conceptually build plant to see how much the cost would be, to see if it's worth going down the steps of feasibility.
"There are a lot of exciting (energy storage) technologies. If and when we find the one for Eskom, it's going to be tremendous for competitiveness," Blake said.
Another Eskom source said the proposal held great promise because it could provide a clean source of energy close to where it was most needed.
"Imagine a 1,000 megawatt plant right near to Johannesburg," the source said.
Mine shafts vary in depth from a few hundred metres to thousands of metres. South Africa, producing most of the world's gold, has some of the deepest gold mine shafts in the world.
The world's biggest gold producer Anglo American Corp of South Africa Ltd is planning to take one of its mines down to depth of 5,000 metres.

According to an Eskom report on research strategy for the five years from 1998, discussions on the "high head underground pumped storage" project have been held with, among others, the Chamber of Mines and the Council for Scientific and Industrial Research.
Adams said Eskom was also studying the possibility of using compressed air pumped into underground mine cavities to provide an energy source for peak hours.
